title: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN)
subject: rheumatology-dermatology
setting: Emergency department, dermatology ward, burns unit, ICU
summary: Stop every suspect drug at once, score SCORTEN, and manage SJS/TEN like a major burn in a specialised unit: warm room, careful fluids, early feeding, analgesia, conservative skin care, daily eye, mouth and genital care, and infection surveillance. Ciclosporin, etanercept and IVIg have limited, mixed evidence.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Prodrome of fever, sore eyes, sore throat and malaise for 1 to 3 days, then painful dusky or purpuric macules and flat atypical targets on the face and trunk that blister and peel in sheets; Nikolsky sign is positive.
Erosions of 2 or more mucosal sites (mouth and lips, eyes, genitals) are almost universal; oral involvement is seen in nearly every case.
Classify by the area of detached or detachable epidermis (not erythema): SJS below 10% of BSA, SJS/TEN overlap 10 to 30%, TEN above 30%.

Usually starts 4 to 28 days after the first dose of the culprit. Common culprits in India: carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, lamotrigine, allopurinol, sulfonamides (co-trimoxazole, sulfasalazine), nevirapine and oxicam NSAIDs; also some antibiotics. Ask about over-the-counter and traditional medicines.
Differentials: erythema multiforme major, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, DRESS, AGEP, generalised bullous fixed drug eruption, autoimmune blistering disease.

sections.title: First hours
items: Stop all suspect and non-essential drugs now. Build a drug timeline (ALDEN helps identify the culprit). Do not switch to another aromatic antiepileptic (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, lamotrigine cross-react); use a non-aromatic agent such as levetiracetam.
Score SCORTEN within 24 hours of admission and again on day 3.

Transfer to a burns unit, ICU or specialist dermatology HDU if more than 10% BSA is detached or SCORTEN is high; manage with a multidisciplinary team (dermatology, ICU or burns, ophthalmology, nursing, nutrition).
IV access through unaffected skin if possible; start warmed crystalloid; urinary catheter for hourly output; strict fluid balance.
Skin biopsy from the edge of a fresh blister for histology, plus perilesional skin for direct immunofluorescence to exclude autoimmune blistering disease.

sections.title: SCORTEN and investigations
items: SCORTEN, 1 point each: age 40 or more; malignancy; heart rate 120/min or more; detached BSA 10% or more; serum urea above 10 mmol/L (BUN above 28 mg/dL, blood urea above about 60 mg/dL); bicarbonate below 20 mmol/L; glucose above 14 mmol/L (252 mg/dL).
Predicted mortality: score 0 to 1 about 3%; 2 about 12%; 3 about 35%; 4 about 58%; 5 or more about 90%. SCORTEN may overestimate mortality.
Bloods: CBC, renal and liver function, glucose, blood gas with bicarbonate, electrolytes including magnesium and phosphate, albumin, CRP, coagulation; chest X-ray.
Swab skin erosions and send blood and urine cultures when infection is suspected; repeat skin swabs regularly until healed.

sections.title: Supportive care (as for burns)
items: Side room with barrier nursing and a warm environment to limit heat loss (BAD 2016 suggests 25 to 28 °C; Latin American guidance 28 to 32 °C); pressure-relieving mattress.

Fluids: titrate IV crystalloid to urine output 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h. Needs are lower than in burns of the same area, so burns formulas overestimate; one estimate for the first 24 hours is 1.5 mL x %BSA x weight in kg (modified Brooke). Avoid overload.
Early enteral nutrition, by mouth if possible or nasogastric if oral intake is too painful.
Analgesia to pain scores: regular paracetamol plus opioids as needed. Avoid NSAIDs (possible culprits).

Skin: handle gently; leave detached epidermis in place as a biological dressing; puncture tense blisters and leave the roof; apply a greasy emollient (for example 50% white soft paraffin with 50% liquid paraffin) to all skin; non-adherent (silicone) dressings on raw areas; no adhesive tape.
No prophylactic antibiotics; treat only clinical infection, guided by cultures. Remove lines and catheters as soon as possible.
LMWH thromboprophylaxis for immobile patients and stress ulcer prophylaxis in ICU.

sections.title: Eye, mouth, genital and airway care
items: Ophthalmology review within 24 hours and then daily in the acute phase: preservative-free lubricant drops about every 2 hours, and topical steroid or antibiotic drops only as advised by the ophthalmologist. Severe disease may need adhesion release or amniotic membrane grafting.
Mouth: white soft paraffin to the lips every 2 hours; anti-inflammatory mouthwash or spray (benzydamine) before meals; antiseptic mouthwash twice daily; gentle suction if needed.
Urogenital: examine daily; apply white soft paraffin; use non-adherent dressings on erosions; urinary catheter; in women arrange gynaecology review to prevent vaginal adhesions and stenosis.
Respiratory: hypoxia, bronchial hypersecretion or airway mucosal involvement needs early ICU review; intubation by an experienced operator.

sections.title: Immunomodulating therapy (limited evidence)
items: No systemic therapy has proven mortality benefit in well-designed trials. Immunomodulation is controversial and specialist-led: decide with a specialist skin failure MDT (BAD 2016), and if used give it early while detachment is still progressing.
Ciclosporin 3 mg/kg/day orally for about 10 days, then taper: supported by observational and open-label data showing lower than predicted mortality. Avoid with renal impairment or active sepsis.

Etanercept 25 mg SC (weight 65 kg or less) or 50 mg SC (above 65 kg) twice weekly until skin healing: in a 2018 randomised trial it gave faster re-epithelialisation and fewer GI bleeds than systemic corticosteroids, with a non-significant lower mortality.
IVIg: conflicting evidence and no clear mortality benefit in meta-analyses; not recommended routinely.

Systemic corticosteroids remain controversial; if used (still common in India), keep courses short and early. Avoid starting them late in established, extensive TEN and avoid prolonged high doses, which increase sepsis.

sections.title: Before discharge and preventing recurrence
items: Record the culprit and cross-reacting drugs as a severe allergy in all records, give the patient a written alert card, and never rechallenge.
Report the reaction to the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI).

HLA-B*15:02 screening before carbamazepine (and consider before oxcarbazepine or phenytoin) in people of South or Southeast Asian ancestry where available; HLA-B*58:01 before allopurinol in high-risk patients.
Follow up for sequelae: dry eye, symblepharon and visual loss (ophthalmology), nail and pigment changes, genital adhesions, and psychological distress.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Continuing the culprit, or switching to another aromatic antiepileptic, while 'observing' the rash.
Mistaking early SJS for a viral exanthem or erythema multiforme and giving NSAIDs for the fever.
Counting erythema in the BSA estimate, or not repeating SCORTEN on day 3.
Burns-formula fluid overload, prophylactic antibiotics, or aggressive debridement of skin.
Delaying ophthalmology review, risking permanent visual loss.

drugs.name: Ciclosporin
drugs.dose: 3 mg/kg/day orally in 2 divided doses for about 10 days, then taper
drugs.notes: Best-supported immunomodulator (observational data). Monitor creatinine and BP; avoid in renal impairment or sepsis.

drugs.name: Etanercept
drugs.dose: 25 mg SC if 65 kg or less, 50 mg SC if above 65 kg, twice weekly until skin healing
drugs.notes: RCT versus corticosteroids showed faster healing; screen for TB when feasible.

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.dose: 40 mg SC once daily (20 mg daily if creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min)
drugs.notes: VTE prophylaxis in immobile patients; inject through intact skin.

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 1 g orally or IV every 6 hours; maximum 4 g/day (3 g/day if weight below 50 kg or liver disease)
drugs.notes: Add opioids for pain as needed. Avoid NSAIDs.

drugs.name: White soft paraffin / liquid paraffin (50:50)
drugs.dose: Apply to all skin and lips frequently (lips every 2 hours)
drugs.notes: Barrier and emollient for the whole epidermis.

drugs.name: Preservative-free ocular lubricant
drugs.dose: 1 to 2 drops each eye about every 2 hours
drugs.notes: Topical steroid or antibiotic drops only on ophthalmology advice.

drugs.name: Benzydamine 0.15% oral rinse or spray
drugs.dose: 15 mL rinse (or spray) every 2 to 3 hours, especially before meals
drugs.notes: Oral pain relief; dilute if stinging.
